paragraphs.text: This is a lab experiment in rats about rearing, which means standing up on the hind legs to look and sniff around. It asks whether the hippocampus, a brain area needed for remembering places, must be working during rearing for rats to remember where they have been.

sentences.text: This is a lab experiment in rats about rearing, which means standing up on the hind legs to look and sniff around.
It asks whether the hippocampus, a brain area needed for remembering places, must be working during rearing for rats to remember where they have been.

paragraphs.text: Most past studies looked at the hippocampus while animals walked or rested quietly. Rearing comes with a strong brain rhythm linked to memory, yet whether rearing matters for place memory was unknown.

sentences.text: Most past studies looked at the hippocampus while animals walked or rested quietly.
Rearing comes with a strong brain rhythm linked to memory, yet whether rearing matters for place memory was unknown.

paragraphs.text: Rats first collected food from four open arms of an eight-arm maze, then later had to find food in the other four. Using light-sensitive brain cells, the team briefly switched off the hippocampus whenever a rat reared during that first visit. Correct first choices fell from 77.7% to 65.7%, and rats needed more arm visits, 6.5 instead of 5.1. Switching it off 6 seconds after rearing caused no clear drop, and rats without the light-sensitive cells were unaffected.

paragraphs.text: The authors conclude that hippocampus activity during rearing is important for place memory. They suggest rearing may help the brain update its inner map of the surroundings.

fuller.text: This is a lab experiment on rats about the hippocampus, a brain area needed for remembering places. While exploring, rats often stop and stand up on their hind legs, which the authors call rearing. The question is whether the hippocampus has to be working during those moments for the rat to remember where it has been.

fuller.text: Most research has looked at the hippocampus while animals walk or rest quietly, not while they rear. Rearing lets a rat see and smell more of its surroundings, and it comes with a strong brain rhythm linked to memory. Yet whether rearing matters for spatial memory was unknown.

sentences.text: Most research has looked at the hippocampus while animals walk or rest quietly, not while they rear.
Rearing lets a rat see and smell more of its surroundings, and it comes with a strong brain rhythm linked to memory.
Yet whether rearing matters for spatial memory was unknown.

fuller.text: Rats first visited four open arms of an eight-arm maze, then after a four-minute break had to find food in the other four. In the first visit, a light shone through thin fibres switched off hippocampus cells, which had been genetically changed to respond, whenever a rat reared. Correct first choices fell from 77.7% to 65.7%, while switching cells off six seconds after each rear caused no significant drop. Rats without the light-sensitive change were unaffected.

Rats without the light-sensitive change were unaffected.

fuller.text: The authors conclude that hippocampus activity during rearing is important for spatial memory. They suggest rearing may help update the rat's inner map of its surroundings. They note it is still unclear whether every rear matters, or whether the same learning could happen without rearing.

brief.text: Rats often stand up on their hind legs to look around, called rearing. This study asks if a brain part called the hippocampus, needed to remember places, matters during rearing. Scientists have mostly studied it while animals walk or rest, so rearing has been a gap.

brief.text: Rats learned which maze arms still held food, and light briefly switched off their hippocampus during each rear. Later, correct choices dropped from about 78% to 66%. Switching it off 6 seconds after rearing did not clearly hurt memory. So brain activity while rearing can be important for remembering places.
